About Paw & Whisker

Paw & Whisker was started by Paul, a pet parent, not a veterinarian. The site is built around a simple idea: people who share their lives with pets often want clear, practical information before they decide what to read, save, or ask their own vet about. The tone here is meant to stay grounded, plain, and useful.

Paul’s cats are part of the story behind the site. Lucky is his black female cat, aged 1. Sugar is his brown-tabby female cat, aged 7. Lucky is curious and playful, while Sugar is calm and observant. That difference is part of why Paw & Whisker tries to make room for different pet personalities and different household situations rather than assuming every pet behaves the same way.

Why I built it: Lucky's infection

An earlier version of this site helped me once. I sent it a photo of a problem on Lucky. The AI told me to see a vet quickly, so I took her in. She had a bad infection and was treated. That is one owner's experience, not a diagnosis, a guarantee or a medical result. AI cannot diagnose your pet, results vary, and when in doubt you should call a vet. Find a vet near you.

What Paw & Whisker is trying to do

The site exists to organise pet information into articles, guides, and practical checks that are easier to read than a long search through scattered sources. Some pages focus on food questions, some compare tools, and some help readers think through whether a product or topic is a good fit for their own pet and routine. The aim is not to overwhelm readers with jargon or pretend that one answer suits every animal.

Paw & Whisker’s original practical research is not a veterinary consultation. It is meant to help a reader understand a topic, spot the limits of what is known, and decide what question to take next to a professional if needed. Where a page discusses a risk, the goal is to describe the issue clearly rather than dress it up as a diagnosis or a promise of what will happen.

How the site is built

One important part of the site is a browser-local pet profile. That means the profile is kept in the user’s browser rather than being presented as a shared public profile. It is intended to make the experience more personalised on the device being used, without turning the site into a social network or a public pet database. Because it is browser-local, the profile experience is tied to the browser and device where it is created or used.

The chat experience is model-generated and sent to an AI provider. That matters because it shapes how answers are produced: the site is not presenting a human-to-human chat with a staff member, and it is not pretending that every response comes from hands-on observation. Readers should treat the chat as a help tool for organising ideas, narrowing questions, and exploring a topic, not as a substitute for a real professional assessment.

The site also includes two daily UTC questions. These are limited in number, which helps define the pace and scope of the interaction. In practical terms, that means the experience is not designed for unlimited back-and-forth. It is meant to be focused and intentional, with room to ask useful questions without giving the impression that the system is an always-on clinical service.

What the site does not claim

Paw & Whisker does not claim to replace veterinary advice. It does not present itself as a clinic, and it does not claim formal editorial oversight from multiple staff members. A single founder maintains the site. That is important context for readers who want to understand who is behind the content and how to interpret it.

The site also does not claim that every article is based on direct testing, direct veterinary review, or formal hands-on product assessment. Where readers see product discussions or comparisons, the value is in the practical framing, the distinctions, and the questions a person can ask when comparing options. For comparison content, public descriptions from competitors may be referenced as part of the comparison, but those are external claims, not hands-on testing by Paw & Whisker.

Some guides cite trusted organisations such as ASPCA, Pet Poison Helpline, AAHA, AKC, Blue Cross, and PDSA. Three older guides were recovered from the owner’s site. That helps explain why the site may include a mix of newer writing and material that has been brought forward from earlier work. Even so, readers should still treat each page as written by the site owner rather than as a formal multi-person publication.

Reviewed by a licensed veterinarian: coming soon

This exact line is part of the site’s About information: Reviewed by a licensed veterinarian: coming soon. It is included here exactly as stated and does not mean the page has already completed veterinary review. Readers should understand it as a future-facing note, not a finished endorsement.

How to use the site well

A practical way to use Paw & Whisker is to read for distinctions rather than looking for a one-size-fits-all answer. For example, a food page may be useful because it helps separate “not toxic” from “still a bad fit for a pet’s digestion or chewing ability.” A tool comparison may be useful because it shows where one product is described more clearly than another, or where a competitor’s public description is vague, while still leaving room for unknowns.

If you are comparing products or reading a checker page, it can help to ask: what problem is this meant to solve, what is left unverified, and what does the page explicitly not know? Those questions matter because they help turn a general overview into a decision aid. They also stop a reader from assuming that a broad description means a product has been fully tested in every situation.

For food-specific topics, the site may link to a tool page under /tools/toxic-food-checker/ rather than a species-specific route. Those tool pages are intended to be clearer entry points for checking a food-related question without pushing the reader into a narrow path that may no longer exist. That keeps the structure simple while still giving the reader a relevant place to start.

Practical limits and reader expectations

Paw & Whisker is intentionally modest about what it can know. If a mechanism is not established in the source material, the site should say so plainly instead of filling the gap with speculation. If timing is not established, it should stay unclaimed. That approach keeps the writing honest and prevents a reader from mistaking uncertainty for certainty.

The same caution applies to comparisons, food topics, and general pet information. If something is unknown or unverified, that is a meaningful answer in itself. It may mean a product has not described a feature clearly, a comparison cannot be made on the evidence provided, or a food issue is more about physical or digestive upset than a true toxic reaction. The site tries to keep those distinctions visible.

Because the founder is a pet parent rather than a veterinarian, the content is best used as a well-organised starting point. It can help you understand what a page is trying to say, what it leaves out, and what kind of follow-up question might be worth asking. That can be especially helpful when a topic is confusing, when different pets behave differently, or when a product claim sounds broader than the evidence behind it.

Contact

If you need to reach Paul, the contact email is paul@pawandwhisker.net.

Short version

Paw & Whisker is a single-founder pet information site created by Paul, a pet parent. It uses a browser-local pet profile, model-generated chat sent to an AI provider, and two daily UTC questions. It includes practical guides and comparisons, with some pages citing recognised pet-health organisations and three older guides recovered from the owner’s site. It is not a veterinary consultation, and the page note Reviewed by a licensed veterinarian: coming soon should be read exactly that way: coming soon, not already complete.
